chapters.name: Chapter 1: Smoke and safety in the kitchen

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How cooking smoke harms your family
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain how cooking smoke harms health and who it hurts most.
This lesson builds toward: Given a kitchen that cooks with firewood, charcoal or kerosene, you will explain how cooking smoke harms health and who it hurts most, naming at least three health effects and the people most exposed.
Smoke from firewood, charcoal, crop waste, dung and kerosene is full of tiny particles and gases. You cannot see most of them, but they go deep into the lungs. This is called household air pollution.
WHO says household air pollution causes pneumonia and other chest infections in children, and stroke, heart disease, long-term lung disease and lung cancer in adults. It is also linked with low birth weight and eye disease. WHO counts about 2.1 billion people worldwide who cook with polluting fuels and stoves, most of them in Africa and Asia.
Women and young children breathe the most smoke, because they spend the most time near the fire, and babies are often carried on the back while the mother cooks. Girls and women also lose hours collecting firewood, time that could go to school, work or rest.
Smoke you cannot see still harms. A smell of smoke, stinging eyes, coughing while cooking, and black walls or roof are signs that your family breathes too much of it.
Words to know:
- Household air pollution: smoke and gases in and around the home, mostly from cooking, heating and lighting with polluting fuels.
- Polluting fuels: fuels that make a lot of smoke when burned in simple stoves: wood, charcoal, crop waste, dung, coal and kerosene.
- Pneumonia: a serious chest infection; it is a leading killer of young children.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Household air pollution (polluting fuels, health effects, clean fuels, kerosene)
Try it now: Watch your kitchen during one meal. Write how long the fire burns, who is near it, whether a baby or young child is there, and the signs of smoke you see. Write three ways the smoke could harm your family.
You can now explain how cooking smoke harms health and who in your home breathes the most.

check.q: Which illness in young children does WHO link with cooking smoke?
check.why: Household air pollution causes lower respiratory infections such as pneumonia.

check.q: Who usually breathes the most cooking smoke?
options: Women who cook and the young children near them
check.why: Women and young children spend the most time near the fire.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Cutting smoke today with what you have
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List steps that cut smoke in your kitchen this week, with the stove you have now.
This lesson builds toward: Using the stove and fuel you have now, you will list steps that cut smoke in your kitchen this week, with at least three steps that cost little or nothing.
A new stove helps most, but you can cut smoke today. Let air in and smoke out: cook outside or under a shelter when you can, keep doors and windows open while cooking, and if you can, make a window, eave gap or chimney opening near the fire.
Burn less and burn cleaner. Use dry wood: wet wood makes much more smoke. Split wood into thin pieces and push it in slowly. Use a lid on the pot, soak beans and maize before cooking, and put out the fire as soon as the food is ready.
Keep children away. Keep babies and young children out of the kitchen while the fire burns, and do not cook with a baby on your back if someone else can hold the baby.
Never burn plastic, rubber or painted wood: their smoke is poisonous.
Step by step:
- Let air in: cook outside or open doors and windows.
- Use dry, split wood and push it in slowly.
- Cover pots; soak beans and maize first.
- Put the fire out when the food is ready.
- Keep babies and young children away from the smoke.
Words to know:
- Ventilation: letting fresh air in and smoky air out.
- Eave gap: an opening between the top of the wall and the roof that lets smoke out.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Household air pollution (polluting fuels, health effects, clean fuels, kerosene)
Try it now: Choose three steps from this lesson you can start this week with no money or very little. Write them down, try them for three days, and note what changed (less smoke, less wood, less time).
You can now cut smoke in your kitchen with steps that cost little or nothing.

check.q: Which wood makes the least smoke?
options: Large logs pushed in all at once
Painted wood from an old door
Dry, thin pieces pushed in slowly
check.why: Dry, thin wood burns more fully and makes less smoke.

check.q: Which step cuts smoke and fuel at the same time?
options: Cooking with a lid on the pot
Leaving the fire burning after cooking
Burning plastic to start the fire
check.why: A lid cooks food faster, so you burn less fuel and make less smoke.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Staying safe with fire, charcoal, gas and kerosene
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Follow safety rules that prevent burns, carbon monoxide poisoning, gas fires and kerosene poisoning.
This lesson builds toward: When cooking with fire, charcoal, gas or kerosene, you will follow safety rules that prevent burns, carbon monoxide poisoning, gas fires and kerosene poisoning, choosing the safe action in at least 4 of 5 situations.
Burns: keep the stove stable and, if you can, raised off the floor with a guard around an open fire. Turn pot handles inward. Keep children away from the cooking area. If someone is burned, WHO first aid is: stop the burning, cool the burn under cool running water (about 20 minutes for small burns), take off rings and tight clothes, and cover it with a clean cloth. Do not put butter, oil, toothpaste or traditional pastes on it. Go to the clinic for large or deep burns, or burns on the face, hands, feet or private parts.
Charcoal: a burning charcoal stove gives off carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can kill. Never bring a burning charcoal stove into a closed room to cook or to warm the room, and never sleep with one inside. Headache, dizziness and sleepiness near the stove are warning signs: get everyone into fresh air.
Gas (LPG): buy cylinders from a licensed seller, keep the cylinder upright, and check the hose and regulator. If you smell gas: do not light a match or turn on any switch, turn off the cylinder valve, open doors and windows, and get people outside. Turn the valve off after cooking.
Kerosene: WHO advises against kerosene for cooking and lighting, and swallowing kerosene is a leading cause of child poisoning. Keep it in a closed, labelled container, never in a drink bottle, and out of children's reach. If a child swallows it, go to the clinic now.
Step by step:
- Keep the stove stable and children away; turn handles inward.
- Never use charcoal in a closed room or while sleeping.
- Gas: licensed seller, upright cylinder, valve off after cooking.
- Smell gas: no flames or switches, valve off, open up, get out.
- Kerosene: labelled container, never a drink bottle, out of reach.
Words to know:
- Carbon monoxide: a poisonous gas from burning fuel; you cannot see or smell it.
- LPG: liquefied petroleum gas: cooking gas sold in cylinders.
- Regulator: the part on top of the gas cylinder that controls the gas going to the stove.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Burns (first aid and prevention at home)
- WHO fact sheet: Household air pollution (polluting fuels, health effects, clean fuels, kerosene)
Try it now: Walk through your kitchen and write five safety rules for your home: one for burns and children, one for charcoal, one for gas or kerosene (whichever you use), one for storing fuel, and one for what to do in an emergency, with the nearest clinic.
You can now cook safely with fire, charcoal, gas and kerosene and act fast if something goes wrong.

check.q: It is cold in Ouagadougou at night. Is it safe to bring the burning charcoal stove into the closed bedroom?
options: Yes, if the door is shut
Yes, if the charcoal is good quality
Yes, if you sleep far from it
No: it gives off carbon monoxide, which can kill
check.why: Carbon monoxide builds up in a closed room and can kill sleeping people.

check.q: You smell gas in the kitchen. What do you do first?
options: Light a match to find the leak
Turn off the valve and open the doors and windows
check.why: No flames or switches; shut off the gas and let it out.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Cleaner stoves and fuels
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Compare cleaner stoves and fuels by smoke, cost, fuel supply and safety.
This lesson builds toward: Given two or more stove and fuel options available where you live, you will compare cleaner stoves and fuels by smoke, cost, fuel supply and safety, with a correct reason for the option you choose.
WHO lists the cleanest options: solar, electricity, biogas, LPG (cooking gas), natural gas, alcohol fuels such as ethanol, and biomass stoves that meet WHO emission targets. WHO advises against kerosene and unprocessed coal.
Improved wood or charcoal stoves (also called efficient or improved cookstoves) burn less fuel and make less smoke than three stones or an open fire. They are a step forward, but most still make a lot of smoke, so keep the kitchen well ventilated. Ask the seller whether the model has been tested.
Gas (LPG) and electric cooking make almost no smoke in the kitchen. An electric pressure cooker or a hot plate can be cheap to run where power is reliable, and is good for beans and stews. Biogas fits a farm with cattle and space for a digester. A retained-heat cooker (a well-insulated basket or box) finishes cooking with no extra fuel and works with any stove.
Choose what fits your place: Is the fuel sold near you all year? Can you pay for refills? Is it safe for your home? In many towns gas or electricity may fit; in villages far from supply, an improved stove plus good ventilation may be the first step.
Step by step:
- List the stoves and fuels sold near you.
- For each, note smoke (a lot, some, almost none).
- Note the fuel supply: always available, sometimes, rarely.
- Note safety needs and the upfront and running cost.
- Pick the cleanest option you can supply and afford.
Words to know:
- Improved cookstove: a wood or charcoal stove designed to burn less fuel and make less smoke than an open fire.
- Biogas: gas made from animal dung and plant waste in a closed tank called a digester.
- Retained-heat cooker: an insulated basket or box that keeps a hot pot cooking without more fuel.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Household air pollution (polluting fuels, health effects, clean fuels, kerosene)
- WHO: Clean Household Energy Solutions Toolkit (clean, transitional and polluting fuels)
- Clean Cooking Alliance
Try it now: Ask at your local market, shop or gas seller which stoves and fuels are sold near you. Make a small table of two or three options with four columns: smoke, fuel supply, safety needs and cost (use the real prices you are told).
You can now compare cleaner stoves and fuels by smoke, cost, fuel supply and safety, and pick one that fits.

check.q: Which of these does WHO list as a clean cooking fuel?
check.why: WHO lists LPG, electricity, biogas, solar and ethanol among clean fuels.

check.q: A family in a village far from any gas seller wants less smoke now. What is a sensible first step?
options: An improved stove plus good ventilation
Buy a gas cylinder they cannot refill
Cook indoors with the windows shut
check.why: An improved stove with ventilation cuts smoke where cleaner fuels are not yet supplied.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Counting the cost and paying for a switch
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate your monthly fuel cost and compare it with the cost of a cleaner option.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own fuel spending and local prices, you will calculate your monthly fuel cost and compare it with the cost of a cleaner option, with the sums correct and the payment risks named.
Many families think clean cooking is too costly, but they never add up what they already spend. Write what you spend on firewood, charcoal or kerosene in a normal week, and multiply by 4 for a rough monthly cost. If you collect wood, also count the hours spent.
For the cleaner option, count two costs: the upfront cost (the stove, the cylinder and regulator) and the running cost (refills or electricity each month). Then compare the running cost with what you spend now, and work out how many months it takes for any saving to pay back the upfront cost.
Example with made-up numbers, not real prices: a family in Kisumu spends KES 300 a week on charcoal, about KES 1,200 a month. A cleaner option costs KES 900 a month to run and KES 3,600 upfront. They save KES 300 a month, so the upfront cost is paid back in 12 months (3,600 divided by 300). Use your own prices.
Ways to pay: save a little each week, buy together through a savings group or chama, tontine or esusu, or ask about pay-as-you-go gas or stove plans offered where you live. Before you sign, ask the full price, what happens if you miss a payment, and who repairs it. Do not pay a stranger who promises a free stove for a fee, and buy gas only from licensed sellers.
Step by step:
- Write your weekly fuel spend and multiply by 4.
- Write the upfront and monthly cost of a cleaner option.
- Subtract to find the monthly saving (or extra cost).
- Divide the upfront cost by the monthly saving to find the months to pay back.
- Choose how to pay and check the terms.
Words to know:
- Upfront cost: the money you pay once at the start, such as for the stove.
- Running cost: the money you pay again and again, such as fuel refills.
- Pay back: the time it takes for savings to cover what you paid at the start.
- Pay-as-you-go: paying in small amounts, often by mobile money, as you use the fuel or stove.
Try it now: Write what your household spends on cooking fuel in a normal week (in your currency, for example NGN, GHS, XOF, XAF or EGP) and work out the month. Then use real prices you found in Lesson 4 to work out the monthly saving and the months to pay back for one cleaner option.
You can now work out what cooking fuel costs you each month and whether a cleaner option pays back.

check.q: Example only: a family spends GHS 50 a week on charcoal. About how much is that a month?
check.why: 50 a week times 4 weeks is about 200 a month.

check.q: A man phones offering a "free government stove" if you first send a fee by mobile money. What is this?
options: A warning sign of a scam; do not pay
check.why: Asking for a fee to receive something free is a common scam sign.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your kitchen safety and switch plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a kitchen safety and switch plan that your household agrees to.
This lesson builds toward: With your household or business, you will write a kitchen safety and switch plan that the household agrees to, with every part filled in and a date to switch.
A plan turns what you learned into action. It has six parts: what you cook with now and its monthly cost; three steps to cut smoke this week; your safety rules; two cleaner options compared; your choice, how you will pay and the date you will switch; and who agreed.
Talk with the whole household. The person who pays and the person who cooks may see things differently. Share what smoke does to the children's chests, the money you counted, and the time saved from collecting wood. Ask everyone what worries them, such as fear of gas or the taste of food, and answer it.
If you run a food business, such as a chop bar in Kumasi, a mama put in Lagos or a dibiterie in Dakar, add your customers and staff: less smoke means a cleaner place and healthier workers, and fuel is often one of your biggest costs.
Put the plan on the wall. After one month, check: is there less smoke, and what did fuel cost? Change the plan if needed.
Step by step:
- Write the six parts of the plan.
- Talk it through with the household or staff.
- Answer their worries.
- Agree the choice, the payment and the switch date.
- Check after one month and adjust.
Words to know:
- Switch plan: a written plan for moving to a cleaner, safer way of cooking.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page kitchen safety and switch plan with all six parts. Talk it through with your household or staff and write the names of who agreed.
You can now write a kitchen safety and switch plan and agree it with your household.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Why it matters No health reason given, or the reasons are wrong. Names at least three health effects of smoke and who in the home breathes the most. Also names time lost collecting fuel and who it affects. Smoke cut this week Fewer than three steps, or steps that cost a lot. Three steps that cost little or nothing, such as ventilation, dry wood and lids. Steps have been tried, with a note of what changed. Safety rules Missing rules for the fuel used, or an unsafe rule. Clear rules for burns and children and for the fuels the household uses, with the nearest clinic. Includes the gas-leak steps or the charcoal carbon monoxide rule, and fuel storage. Options compared Only one option, or no comparison. Two options compared on smoke, fuel supply, safety and cost, with a correct reason for the choice. Prices come from real local sellers and fuel supply is checked. Cost and payment No monthly cost, or the sums are wrong. Monthly fuel cost now, the cleaner option's costs and a payment way, with correct sums. Shows the months to pay back and names the questions to ask before signing. Plan agreed No switch date, or nobody else has seen it. All six parts are filled in, with a switch date and the names of who agreed. Includes a one-month check of smoke and cost. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which belongs in a kitchen switch plan?
options: A date to switch and how you will pay
Only the colour of the stove
A promise to cook indoors with charcoal
check.why: The plan needs a choice, a payment plan and a date to make the switch happen.

check.q: The person who cooks wants gas, but the person who pays is worried about cost. What helps most?
options: Show the monthly fuel cost you counted and the health facts
check.why: Real numbers and health facts help the household agree.
